candidates.speaker: Maurya
candidates.quote: No man at all can be living for ever, and we must be satisfied.
candidates.author: J. M. Synge
candidates.locator: the one-act play, its closing line, the end of Maurya’s last speech; read verbatim in the Project Gutenberg text; first printed in Samhain (October 1903), then Elkin Mathews (1905)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The last sentence of the play takes the plainest measure of mortality there is and then chooses contentment, which is where gratitude begins.

candidates.speaker: Tyltyl
candidates.author: Maurice Maeterlinck
candidates.locator: Act V, scene 2, The Graveyard, the last line of the scene, Tyltyl answering Mytyl’s Where are the dead? as the graves flower at dawn; read in the Project Gutenberg text of the six-act edition (translator’s note dated 14 November 1910), which prints four points after dead, cut to a full stop as the shipped Act IV line was
candidates.whyThisMonth: The children open the graves at midnight and find a garden at sunrise, so the month’s mortality card can also be a morning one.

candidates.speaker: E. M. Ashford
candidates.quote: Nothing but a breath—a comma—separates life from life everlasting. It is very simple really.
candidates.author: Margaret Edson
candidates.locator: the flashback in which Professor E. M. Ashford corrects the student Vivian Bearing on the punctuation of Donne’s Death be not proud, pp. 14 to 15 (Faber and Faber, 1999); wording from a study-guide quotation keyed to those pages, the printed page not opened, confidence medium
candidates.whyThisMonth: A scholar’s correction of a comma becomes the gentlest account of the last things in modern drama: a pause, not a full stop.

candidates.speaker: Peter
candidates.quote: To die will be an awfully big adventure.
candidates.author: J. M. Barrie
candidates.locator: Act III, The Mermaids’ Lagoon, the close of the act as the rock goes under, with a drum beating in his breast (Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1928); read verbatim in the Project Gutenberg text of that edition; the line was added to the play in 1905
candidates.whyThisMonth: The boy who will not grow up meets the thought of the end with curiosity instead of dread, which is a brave way to open a November day.

candidates.speaker: Nicholas
candidates.quote: To the family—that dear octopus from whose tentacles we never quite escape, nor, in our inmost hearts, ever quite wish to.
candidates.author: Dodie Smith
candidates.locator: Act III, Nicholas Randolph’s toast at the golden-wedding dinner, the speech that gives the play its title (William Heinemann, 1938); the play text was not opened and the wording is the one the reference entry and two reviews agree on, confidence medium
candidates.whyThisMonth: A toast at a golden wedding, it is thanks for family in the form everyone recognises, half rueful and wholly grateful.

candidates.quote: O let the soul her slumbers break, / Let thought be quickened, and awake; / Awake to see / How soon this life is past and gone, / And death comes softly stealing on, / How silently!
candidates.author: Jorge Manrique
candidates.work: Coplas por la muerte de su padre (Coplas de Manrique)
candidates.locator: stanza 1, the opening of the poem, in Longfellow’s translation first published as Coplas de Don Jorge Manrique (Allen and Ticknor, Boston, 1833); read verbatim in the Project Gutenberg Complete Poetical Works
candidates.whyThisMonth: Its first word is a waking: it asks the soul to rise and see how quietly time goes, which is the month’s theme set at the hour it is read.

candidates.quote: Drift on the Stream of Infinite Flux, / Without joy, without fear: / When you must go—then go, / And make as little fuss as you can.
candidates.author: Tao Yuanming
candidates.locator: Spirit expounds, the last four lines, the close of the poem, in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (Constable, 1918); read verbatim in the Project Gutenberg text, whose double hyphen is Waley’s dash
candidates.whyThisMonth: The oldest calm counsel on mortality in this lane, it lightens the subject with a smile: go when it is time, and make no fuss.

candidates.quote: In this world / we walk on the roof of hell, / gazing at flowers.
candidates.author: Kobayashi Issa
candidates.work: yo no naka wa jigoku no ue no hanami kana (In this world)
candidates.locator: the hokku, the Issa section of Robert Hass, The Essential Haiku: Versions of Bashō, Buson, and Issa (Ecco Press, 1994); wording agrees across three reprints credited to Hass, the Ecco page not opened
candidates.whyThisMonth: Three lines hold both halves of the month: the ground under us is not safe, and the flowers are worth looking at anyway.

candidates.quote: There’s no life / that couldn’t be immortal / if only for a moment. / Death / always arrives by that very moment too late.
candidates.author: Wisława Szymborska
candidates.locator: lines 40 to 44 of 48, the two stanzas before the close, in View with a Grain of Sand (Harcourt Brace, 1995); first in Ludzie na moście (1986); read in the Babel Web Anthology text credited to Cavanagh and Barańczak, the Harcourt page not opened
candidates.whyThisMonth: She turns the fear of death on its head: every life has already had its immortal moment, and death always arrives too late to take it.

candidates.quote: And the miraculous comes so close / to the ruined, dirty houses— / something not known to anyone at all, / but wild in our breast for centuries.
candidates.author: Anna Akhmatova
candidates.locator: the closing stanza, lines 9 to 12, Poems of Akhmatova (Little, Brown, 1973); read in the reprint in Jane Hirshfield’s anthology Women in Praise of the Sacred (1994); written June 1921, first in Anno Domini MCMXXI (1922)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Written in the ruin of 1921, it finds the miraculous right beside the dirty houses, which is gratitude that has not looked away from anything.

candidates.quote: A day so happy. / Fog lifted early, I worked in the garden. / Hummingbirds were stopping over honeysuckle flowers. / There was no thing on earth I wanted to possess.
candidates.author: Czesław Miłosz
candidates.locator: lines 1 to 4 of 9, the poem dated Berkeley 1971, in The Collected Poems 1931 to 1987 (Ecco Press, 1988); read in the Scottish Poetry Library text credited to New and Collected Poems 1931 to 2001 (2001); the individual translator credit was not seen
candidates.whyThisMonth: An old man’s perfect morning in a garden, set down plainly, is a model of thanks that asks for nothing more.

candidates.quote: When it’s over, I want to say: all my life / I was a bride married to amazement. / I was the bridegroom, taking the world into my arms.
candidates.author: Mary Oliver
candidates.locator: lines 21 to 23 of 28, New and Selected Poems (Beacon Press, 1992); the colon after say is in most reprints and missing from a few, the Beacon page not opened, confidence medium
candidates.whyThisMonth: The poem that begins with death arriving like a hungry bear ends by naming the only verdict worth wanting: a life married to amazement.

candidates.quote: come celebrate / with me that everyday / something has tried to kill me / and has failed.
candidates.author: Lucille Clifton
candidates.locator: the closing lines, from the middle of line 11 to line 14, The Book of Light (Copper Canyon Press, 1993); read in the Poetry Foundation text credited to that edition; the poem is lower case throughout
candidates.whyThisMonth: An invitation to celebrate plain survival, it makes the ordinary fact of waking up a small victory worth giving thanks for.

candidates.quote: O world, I cannot hold thee close enough! / Thy winds, thy wide grey skies! / Thy mists, that roll and rise!
candidates.author: Edna St. Vincent Millay
candidates.locator: lines 1 to 3, the opening, Renascence and Other Poems (Mitchell Kennerley, 1917); read verbatim in the Project Gutenberg text
candidates.whyThisMonth: Written on an autumn day, it is gratitude too large for the speaker to hold, and it suits a November window at first light.

candidates.quote: And did you get what / you wanted from this life, even so? / I did. / And what did you want? / To call myself beloved, to feel myself / beloved on the earth.
candidates.author: Raymond Carver
candidates.locator: the whole poem, the last in A New Path to the Waterfall (Atlantic Monthly Press, 1989); lineation checked in one reprint crediting the book and the wording in a second, the Atlantic page not opened
candidates.whyThisMonth: Written near the end and cut on his gravestone, it asks the last question of a life and answers it with the whole of gratitude: I did.

candidates.quote: I strove with none, for none was worth my strife. / Nature I loved and, next to Nature, Art: / I warm’d both hands before the fire of life; / It sinks, and I am ready to depart.
candidates.author: Walter Savage Landor
candidates.work: Finis (Dying Speech of an Old Philosopher)
candidates.locator: the whole poem, no. 576 in The Oxford Book of English Verse (ed. Arthur Quiller-Couch, Clarendon Press, 1900), read verbatim in the Project Gutenberg text; first in The Examiner, 1849, and the pointing differs between printings
candidates.whyThisMonth: Written on a birthday late in life, four lines count what he loved, warm both hands at the fire, and leave without complaint: the month in miniature.
